content:
The floating barriers installed in the Río Bravo between Nuevo Laredo and Laredo are cutting off the movement of fish, land animals and some birds, breaking the biological corridors wildlife uses to feed, shelter and reproduce on both sides of the border, according to El Mañana de Nuevo Laredo.

Where the river runs shallow and low — including near Bridge II — the buoys sit on the riverbed instead of floating, effectively splitting the river so fish cannot move freely from one side to the other, the paper reports. Nets and cables attached to the barrier can entangle fish, turtles and aquatic mammals such as otters and beavers and cause injuries, while the structure slows water flow, alters riverside vegetation and the shape of the river, and can damage the refuge and reproduction areas wildlife depends on.

Environmental consultant Gustavo Pantoja, formerly head of the Centro Internacional de Estudios del Río Bravo, warned that the barriers can obstruct flow during high water and contribute to flooding. He said work in the federal zone requires bilateral agreements and urged Mexico's Comisión Internacional de Límites y Aguas and the Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores to intervene and seek solutions for the shared river.

Tricia Cortez, executive director of the Rio Grande International Study Center, had repeatedly warned that the structures threatened public safety, bridge integrity and the regional ecosystem, according to the report. During flooding last July, an upstream section broke loose and was carried by the current toward the two Laredos. The article also notes citizen protests, disapproval from the mayors of both Laredos, and the local CILA representation's position that no permits for the work had been processed — making the measure unilateral. The article gave no buoy count or dollar figure.

What to watch next: whether CILA and the SRE respond to the call for intervention, and how the barrier holds up as the river rises and falls through the rest of the season.

Sources: El Mañana de Nuevo Laredo, “Estorbosas barreras: pegan boyas a la flora y la fauna del río Bravo,” October 25, 2026.

excerpt: Floating barriers in the Río Bravo are blocking wildlife movement and breaking feeding, shelter and reproduction corridors, El Mañana reports — with warnings about flood risk and a call for CILA and the SRE to intervene.
title: Buoy barrier in the Río Bravo blocks wildlife corridors, threatens river ecosystem, experts warn
